UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                              )
    Commonwealth Edison Company               )   Docket No.    ER26-3257-001
                                              )

               MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER
         OF POWERHOUSE HILLWOOD HOLDING LLC TO REQUEST FOR
             REHEARING OF COMMONWEALTH EDISON COMPANY

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of

the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”), 1 PowerHouse

Hillwood Holding LLC (“PHH” or “Hillwood”) hereby moves for leave to answer, and

answers, the Request for Rehearing of Commonwealth Edison Company

(“ComEd”) 2 relating to the Commission’s Order Rejecting Notice of Cancellation of

an effective Transmission Security Agreement (“TSA”) between ComEd and

PHH. 3

I.        INTRODUCTION

          ComEd’s Request for Rehearing should be denied. The Commission

rejected ComEd’s Notice of Cancellation after applying long-standing precedent to

decline to resolve a contract dispute PHH and ComEd are litigating in federal

district court. ComEd now asks the Commission to reverse course on arguments

ComEd did not make earlier, on a factual premise its own filings contradict, and on

a theory that would unsettle decades of Commission practice. In particular:



1
     18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213.
2
 Commonwealth Edison Co., Docket No. ER26-3257-001, Request for Rehearing of
Commonwealth Edison Company (filed Oct. 22, 2026)(“Request for Rehearing”).
3
    Commonwealth Edison Co., 196 FERC ¶ 61,226 (2026)(“Cancellation Rejection Order”).
       •   The Commission was not convinced that ComEd’s cancellation of a
          retail application was a permissible reason to cancel another ComEd
          TSA. ComEd sought to cancel a TSA between it and Red Energy Partners
          LLC (“Red Energy”) on the sole ground that the underlying retail service
          application had been cancelled, 4 the same theory it advances here. The
          Commission rejected the filing without finding it unjust and unreasonable
          because ComEd had not identified any TSA provision making an active
          retail service application a condition of effectiveness. 5 ComEd now asks the
          Commission to hold both that a cancelled retail application by itself justifies
          cancelling a TSA, and that rejecting a section 205 cancellation without a
          justness finding is contrary to law. The Commission’s order on the Red
          Energy cancellation defeats both premises. 6
      •   ComEd incorrectly states the dispute in the District Court is stayed
          when the dispute is in active court litigation. As ComEd is very well
          aware, the parties in the District Court remain in active litigation. The case
          is not stayed. The Commission’s description of the litigation as ongoing was
          accurate. 7
      •   ComEd’s principal section 205 argument appears for the first time on
          rehearing. ComEd impermissibly made its Federal Power Act (“FPA”)
          Section 205(d) and 205(e), its tolling, and five-month suspension limitation
          arguments, as well as introduced arguments under Allegheny Defense
          Project v. FERC, 8 Semtek International Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp. 9 and
          Fairless Energy, LLC v. FERC 10 for the first time on rehearing.

        •   The authority ComEd relies upon does not support its position.
           Atlantic City Electric Company v. FERC 11 concerned whether the
           Commission could strip utilities of their filing rights and reform existing
           contracts. It did not address a filing whose justness depends on first
           resolving a contested contract right as is the case here.
       •   ComEd’s exclusive-jurisdiction authorities concern arrangements
           that are exclusively wholesale. PHH is a retail customer, as ComEd and
           the Commission have acknowledged.
       •   The TSA is governed by Illinois law, as ComEd proposed. ComEd asks
           the Commission to claim special expertise that it does not have in state
           contract law.
       •   ComEd asks the Commission to set aside Arkla. ComEd’s position that
           section 205 forecloses any Commission exercise of discretion to leave a
           contract dispute to be decided in court would invalidate every order in which
           the Commission has declined primary jurisdiction over a cancellation notice.
           ComEd invokes the rule that an agency must explain a departure from
           precedent while asking the Commission to depart from a framework it has
           applied for decades, and the D.C. Circuit applied in a case ComEd itself
           relies on. 12
       •   ComEd’s own retail tariff secures the development costs it says
           customers will bear. As ComEd explained to the Commission, its Illinois
           tariff requires a Large Demand Project applicant to provide deposits
           securing long lead material procurement and engineering costs. 13 ComEd
           invoked those provisions here and holds PHH’s deposits. 14 Cost recovery
           is also not automatic: only a regulator may permit a utility to pass its costs
           to other customers.
II.        ANSWER TO REQUEST FOR REHEARING




11
      Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2002)(“Atlantic City Electric”).
12
  See Ark. La. Gas Co. v. Hall, 7 FERC ¶61,175, at 61,322, reh'g denied, 8 FERC ¶
61,031 (1979) (“Arkla”).
13
  Commonwealth Edison Co., Docket No. ER26-3257-000, Motion for Leave to Answer
and Answer of Commonwealth Edison Company at 4-5 (filed Sept. 1. 2026) (“ComEd
September 1 Answer”).
14
      Id. at 8-9.


                                                 3
           A. The Commission Rejected ComEd’s Notice, Which Is the
             Disposition ComEd Says Section 205 Requires.

          ComEd’s first argument is that the Commission “must ‘accept or reject [a]

proposal.’” 15 ComEd theorizes (wrongly) that the Commission did not do so in the

Order. The Commission, however, rejected the proposal, making this clear in the

opening paragraph, in the body of the Order, in the ordering paragraph, and in a

concurrence. 16 ComEd received one of the two dispositions it says the statute

permits. ComEd’s response is to recharacterize the rejection as a dismissal,

relying on Semtek for the proposition that “[a]n ‘adjudication upon the merits’ is the

opposite of a ‘dismissal without prejudice.’” 17 Semtek construes Federal Rule of

Civil Procedure 41(b) and addresses whether a dismissal precludes claims in a

subsequent action. 18 It does not concern an agency’s disposition of a tariff filing,

and ComEd improperly raises it for the very first time on rehearing. The

Cancellation Rejection Order is a rejection, not a dismissal, and ComEd identifies

no authority holding that a rejection must be with prejudice.

          The D.C. Circuit has confirmed that a rejection without prejudice is a

permissible and reviewable Commission disposition where a contractual predicate

remains unresolved. In Michigan Electric Transmission Co. v. FERC, the

Commission “declined to determine ownership rights and rejected the [generator


15

Ordering ¶ (“[t]he proposed Notice of Cancellation is hereby rejected”); id. (Rosner,

Cancellation.”).

18

concluding that no agreement the petitioner identified “conclusively determined

ownership rights.” 19 The court agreed with the Commission’s reading of the

agreements and denied the petitions for review. 20 There, as here, the Commission

declined to resolve a contested contract question and rejected the filing without

prejudice rather than deciding the underlying rights. The D.C. Circuit treated that

disposition as a final, reviewable order and sustained it. ComEd identifies no

authority holding such a disposition unlawful.

          B. The Commission Relied on On-Point Precedents that Remain
             Good Law.

          ComEd dismisses the three orders the Commission relied on in the Order

as “decades old and unappealed” and as lacking “meaningful analysis.” 21 Each

addressed the same question presented here: a section 205 notice of cancellation

that could not be resolved without first determining a contested contract question.

In Trigen-Syracuse, the Commission explained that “before making a

determination on whether the proposed partial cancellation is just and reasonable,

the Commission, or some other tribunal, must first determine whether Trigen has

the right to unilaterally terminate the contract,” and “[s]ince both the Commission

and the state court have jurisdiction over this issue, we will apply the three-part

test developed in Arkla.” 22

  Mich. Elec. Transmission Co. v. FERC, 141 F.4th 1296, 1299, 1301 (D.C. Cir. 2025)
(describing Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 185 FERC ¶ 61,182 (2023)).

           In PPL Electric, the Commission likewise explained that “[b]ecause of the

necessity of resolving the underlying contractual dispute before we can determine

whether the notice of cancellation was validly filed here for review under FPA

Section 205,” it would “decline to assert primary jurisdiction to address the

threshold issue” and “instead leave this issue to a court of law,” noting that “[b]oth

the Commission and the District Court thus have jurisdiction over this question.” 23

These are not orders that failed to analyze the question. They analyzed it and

reached the same conclusion the Commission reached here.

          Neither the age of an order nor the absence of an appeal diminishes its

authority. ComEd invokes the rule that an agency must explain a departure from

precedent; 24 that rule applies to the orders ComEd asks the Commission to

disregard. And far from being stale, the framework those orders used was applied

by the D.C. Circuit in recent years. 25 Additionally, the Commission applied the

same disposition to another ComEd TSA weeks before the Order here, rejecting

an unopposed notice of cancellation without prejudice. 26




notice of cancellation “without prejudice to it being re-filed after conclusion of court
proceedings”).
23
     PPL Elec. Utils. Corp., 92 FERC ¶ 61,057, at 61,147 (2000).
24

25

Edison Co., No. 1:26-cv-08860, Dkt. 116 at 9 n.6 (N.D. Ill. Oct. 15, 2026) (ComEd
describing that order)(“ComEd Opposition”).


                                             6
           C. Atlantic City Electric Describes the Procedure for Rate Changes,
             and Its Holding Limits the Commission’s Power Over Bargained-
             For Terms.

          ComEd’s principal authority is Atlantic City Electric, for the proposition that

the Commission “can reject [a filing] only if it finds that the changes proposed by

the public utility are not ‘just and reasonable.’” 27 That sentence is entirely dicta and

appears in a passage summarizing the operation of FPA section 205(d) at the

outset of an opinion addressing different questions: whether the Commission could

require transmission owners to cede their section 205 filing rights, whether it could

assert section 203 jurisdiction over withdrawal from an independent system

operator, and whether it could order generic reformation of existing contracts

without the findings Mobile-Sierra requires. The court was not presented with, and

did not address, a filing whose justness and reasonableness could not be

assessed without first resolving a contested question of contract right, as is the

case here.

          In the Order here, the Commission explicitly explained that “it is relevant

whether ComEd has the right to unilaterally terminate the Transmission Security

Agreement in these circumstances,” and that the Parties “disagree as to how key

terms of the Transmission Security Agreement should be interpreted.” 28 Where the

justness of a proposed cancellation turns on a disputed contract right, the

Commission’s own precedent from notices of cancellation filed under section 205

supplies the answer, as Section B above explains.



27
     Atlantic City Electric, 295 F.3d at 9.
28
     Cancellation Rejection Order at P 26.


                                              7
           What Atlantic City Electric actually held is that the Commission exceeded

its authority by compelling transmission owners to surrender their section 205 filing

rights, by asserting section 203 jurisdiction over withdrawal from an independent

system operator, and by ordering generic reformation of pre-existing contracts

without the particularized findings Mobile-Sierra requires. 29 The decision is a

limitation on the Commission’s power to disturb bargained-for contract terms, not

a mandate that the Commission adjudicate every contract dispute a party places

before a court.

          Atlantic City Electric also forecloses the premise on which ComEd’s section

205 argument rests. The court held that “utilities may choose to voluntarily give up,

by contract, some of their rate-filing freedom under section 205,” and that “parties

may negotiate a fixed-rate contract with a provision relinquishing their right to file

for a unilateral change in rates.” 30 The TSA does exactly that: its Section 7(C)(b)

states that, absent written agreement of the Parties, “this TSA shall not be subject

to change by application of any Party pursuant to Section 205 or 206 of the Federal

Power Act,” and specifies the Mobile-Sierra public interest standard for a contested

change. Whether that provision reaches a notice of cancellation is itself a question

of contract interpretation, and it is one the Commission declined to reach. 31 The

section 205 right ComEd describes as unqualified is one the D.C. Circuit has held




29
     Atlantic City Electric, 295 F.3d at 8-11, 11-14, 14-15.
30

31

 may be constrained by agreement, precisely the task the Commission left to the

court to construe under the Illinois law the TSA invokes for doing so. 32

          D. ComEd’s Section 205 Timing Argument Was Not Raised
             Previously.

          ComEd’s second enumerated issue is that the Commission, by rejecting the

Notice without prejudice, “has indefinitely suspended ComEd’s proposed rate

change, contrary to FPA Section 205.” 33 It invokes FPA sections 205(d) and

205(e), the five-month suspension limitation, and Allegheny Defense Project v.

FERC in making this argument. Neither this argument nor any citations to these

cases appear in ComEd’s previous voluminous pleadings filed in the docket. In its

Notice of Cancellation and two answers totalling sixty-eight pages, ComEd cited

neither 16 U.S.C. § 824d(d) nor § 824d(e), never referred to tolling or to the sixty-

day period as a constraint on the Commission, and never cited Allegheny Defense.

The Commission does not entertain arguments raised for the first time on

rehearing that could have been presented earlier, and should reject these

arguments for that reason. 34 The Commission has concluded raising such new

          ComEd’s only reference to the sixty-day period below was a request that

the Commission waive it so that cancellation could take effect the day after (its

concerned Natural Gas Act tolling orders that took “no action on the application

other than buying the Commission more time” and thereby staved off judicial

review. 38 The Commission acted here. It issued an order, ComEd sought

rehearing, and judicial review will be available in due course. Nothing was

suspended, instead the Notice explicitly was rejected. 39

          Nor is it the case that ComEd could not have raised this issue earlier

because it first arose as of the issuance of the Order. PHH asked the Commission

 to decline primary jurisdiction under Arkla, and ComEd opposed that request.

ComEd also addressed the prior orders in which the Commission had declined

primary jurisdiction over cancellation notices, describing them as decisions made

“as a matter of discretion.” 40 Finally, ComEd’s own course of action confirms that

a rejection without prejudice is not the trap it describes. Four days before the Order

here, the Commission rejected ComEd’s Red Energy notice without prejudice.

ComEd then obtained the customer’s consent to that TSA cancellation and

refiled. 41

          E. The Commission’s Authority to Decline Primary Jurisdiction Is
             Settled, as ComEd Previously Acknowledged.

          ComEd argues that the Commission cannot decline to exercise primary

jurisdiction. In caselaw ComEd itself relies upon, the D.C. Circuit disagreed,

stating: “[w]hether to exercise primary jurisdiction is a matter solely within the

Commission’s discretion.” 42 In Fairless Energy, the court affirmed the

Commission’s decision to exercise primary jurisdiction, observing that the court

“has not previously had an occasion to reverse the Commission’s decision to

exercise primary jurisdiction” and declining to do so there. 43 A decision deferring

to the Commission’s choice does not establish that the Commission must make

the opposite choice here.

           Moreover, ComEd previously recognized the Commission had discretion

and cannot now inconsistently argue that it does not. In its September 1, 2026

answer, ComEd described the Commission’s prior declinations as “orders where

the Commission, as a matter of discretion, declined to exercise primary jurisdiction

over contract disputes.” 44 It then argued that “the Arkla factors are easily met,” 45

an argument available only if the Commission had discretion to weigh them.

ComEd now contends the Commission had no authority to weigh anything. 46

          ComEd’s remaining argument on this point is that primary jurisdiction

“applies where a claim is originally cognizable in the courts,” and that the claim

here is “cognizable in no court.” 47 Fairless Energy quotes the same passage from

Western Pacific and then applies the Arkla factors to a contract dispute. 48 ComEd’s

argument is tantamount to alleging that Fairless Energy was wrongly decided. The

contract dispute between the parties is very much cognizable in court, by the TSA’s

own terms. It provides: after negotiation and senior-officer escalation, “either Party

may exercise all remedies available at law or in equity under this TSA, including

the initiation of court proceedings,” and the Parties “stipulate that venue is in

          F. ComEd’s Exclusive-Jurisdiction Authorities Concern Agreements
             with Wholesale, not Retail, Customers.

          ComEd’s third enumerated issue rests on three decisions. 50 Each concerns

wholesale rates. Nantahala Power & Light Company v. Thornburg holds that

“FERC has exclusive jurisdiction over the rates to be charged [to] Nantahala’s

interstate wholesale customers.” 51 Mississippi Power & Light Company v.

Mississippi ex rel. Moore holds that “FERC has exclusive authority to determine

the reasonableness of wholesale rates.” 52 The passage ComEd quotes from In re

FirstEnergy Solutions Corporation concerns “wholesale power rates, terms, and

conditions of service.” 53

          PHH is not a wholesale customer. ComEd told the Commission so when it

filed the TSA: PHH “will be a ComEd retail customer that will not take transmission

service under the PJM Tariff but will be served exclusively under ComEd’s state

jurisdictional retail tariff.” 54 The Commission accepted the TSA on that

understanding and noted that “the ICC retains authority to establish terms of retail

Commission’s exclusive authority over wholesale rates do not establish exclusive

authority over a bilateral security agreement with a retail customer.

          ComEd’s own regulatory conduct proves this point. ComEd sought and

obtained authority from the Illinois Commerce Commission (“ICC”) to require a

TSA as a condition of retail service, and its retail tariff now provides that “[a] TSA

that is on file with, or otherwise approved by, FERC and effective is a condition of

the Company’s commencement of retail service to a Large Demand Project

Applicant or project.” 56 A requirement ComEd asked a state commission to impose

is not a subject over which this Commission has exclusive jurisdiction.

          G. The Retail Application Ground Does Not Support Cancellation.

          As noted above, days before issuing the Order, the Commission rejected a

materially identical ComEd filing seeking to cancel a different TSA. In Red Energy,

ComEd submitted a notice of cancellation of a TSA on the sole basis that “the

underlying retail service application has been cancelled,” and requested waiver of

the sixty-day notice requirement to permit an effective date one day after filing. 57

No party intervened or protested. 58 The Commission nevertheless rejected the

filing without prejudice, explaining:

          ComEd explains only that the underlying retail service application
          “has been cancelled.” However, ComEd does not explain why

           That holding addresses ComEd’s second argument directly. ComEd

contends here that “the Commission could have accepted the Notice based on the

terminated Retail Application alone.” 60 The Commission disagreed, holding that

cancellation of a retail service application does not by itself necessarily support

cancellation of a TSA, and indicating ComEd had identified no provision of the TSA

to that effect.

           The same deficiency is present here. ComEd asserts that this TSA

“unambiguously conditions its effectiveness on an active Retail Application.” 61

Unlike in Red Energy, ComEd has cited provisions of the TSA but none of them

states the condition ComEd claims. The provisions ComEd relies on are the

agreement’s recitals, which it says are incorporated into the terms and conditions,

and section 3(D). 62 The TSA recitals describe PHH’s intent to interconnect “for the

purpose of taking retail electric delivery services,” and TSA Section 13 provides

that upon expiry of the Term “Customer may elect to receive” service “pursuant to

the Retail Service Tariff.” 63 Section 3(D) provides that ComEd will work to meet

the requested Commercial Operation Date “consistent with Good Utility Practice,

its retail service obligations, and applicable Retail Service Tariffs.” None of these

effectiveness, and none provides that ComEd may cancel the agreement upon

          Nor does ComEd contend that PHH is barred from submitting a new retail

service application. The agreement assumes the contrary: Sections 4(D) and

14(H) condition the Customer’s termination right on an application that has “not

[been] renewed or reinitiated,” language that presupposes renewal is available. 64

A condition the counterparty may restore is not one whose absence renders an

agreement purposeless.

          ComEd separately asserts that “the Commission’s regulations require

cancelling a rate” in these circumstances. 65 Section 35.15(a) prescribes how a

notice of cancellation is to be filed and when. It identifies no circumstance in which

cancellation is required, and it does not direct the Commission to accept one.

ComEd read the provision the same way earlier in this proceeding. It cited section

35.15 for the procedural question of when a cancellation notice must be filed, and

asked the Commission to waive that filing period, relief that would be unnecessary

if the provision instead compelled cancellation on demand. 66
